# The AI-Native Design Life Cycle {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> "All models are wrong but some are useful."
>
> — George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* [@Box1979Robustness, p. 202]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *Once an AI-native design system is being considered, how should the design work be organized, and why does that structure matter?*

**Core thesis:** *AI-native design requires an explicit six-stage lifecycle (Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit), linked by structured execution records rather than ad hoc prompt sequences.*
:::

An AI-native design system cannot rely on conversational improvisation or ad hoc script chains. Generating hundreds of architectural candidates an hour accelerates progress only if the surrounding system can systematically compile, simulate, physically evaluate, and causally diagnose those proposals without losing provenance or burning human engineering bandwidth. This chapter organizes that discipline into an explicit six-stage life cycle: Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit (@fig-ch03-cover-map). Each stage answers a distinct engineering obligation, from bounding the physical design space to establishing what returned metrics justify doing next.

These stages are not bureaucratic check-boxes; they are inspectable contractual boundaries that prevent catastrophic failure escalation across abstraction seams. Empirical defect telemetry across open silicon engineering projects proves that allowing unvetted architectural candidates to escape into late-stage physical signoff multiplies triage latency by an order of magnitude. Through a concrete walkthrough of a neural processing unit (NPU) accumulator block in the prospective Lighthouse system-on-chip (SoC), this chapter demonstrates how structured execution records maintain causal lineage from architectural intent to physical signoff, ensuring that surprises on the cluster floor route back to the exact assumption that failed.

![**Six life-cycle responsibilities establish inspectable handoffs.** The design process progresses through Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit. Targeted feedback routes unexpected outcomes or inadequate evidence back to the specific prior responsibility that owns the shortfall, maintaining explicit provenance across human and automated contributions.](images/ch03-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch03-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which six life-cycle activities run from formulation through review and decision. Feedback returns work to earlier activities for investigation and revision."}

## The Six Stages of the AI-Native Life Cycle {#sec-arch2-ontology}

The pressures in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales affect the whole path from a design idea to an engineering decision. Generating alternatives more quickly helps only if the team can implement them, compare them under meaningful conditions, and use the results to decide what to try next. The life cycle connects those activities so that progress in one can inform the others.

Separating requirements, design alternatives, implementation, and verification has precedents in systems engineering, where these activities are iterative and interdependent [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook, chap. 4]. The six stages used here are the book's organization of recurring architecture work. Their usefulness rests on whether they help a reader follow a design, identify what the results establish, and decide what needs revision. They need not correspond to six teams, six software components, or six consecutive steps in every tool flow. A stage is a sequential position in that life cycle; a responsibility is the ownership a repair routes back to, which is why a later review in Commit can re-enter Formulate's responsibility without confusing the two.

Consider a candidate that misses its clock-frequency target. The target may be unrealistic, the microarchitecture may need revision, or the analysis may have used the wrong constraints. These explanations call for different next steps. A stage boundary helps expose what was assumed, what ran, and what was learned; it does not diagnose the failure by itself. Existing milestones such as register-transfer level (RTL) freeze and timing signoff remain in place. The stages describe work that can recur before and between those milestones.

Empirical evidence from open silicon engineering projects underscores why isolating stage boundaries is vital. Across 4,564 closed engineering issues from lowRISC OpenTitan, OpenROAD, and Chipyard, defect triage and resolution latency escalates by over an order of magnitude across life-cycle seams (@fig-lifecycle-defect-latency). While front-end build and generator defects resolve in days, defects that escape across abstraction seams into physical static timing analysis (STA) signoff, post-silicon validation, and hardware-software toolchain boundaries take months, incurring an 8.0× to 11.5× resolution latency multiplier relative to front-end synthesis.

![**Defect resolution latency escalates by an order of magnitude across life-cycle seams.** (a) Across 4,564 closed silicon issues in lowRISC OpenTitan, OpenROAD, and Chipyard, median resolution latency rises from 22.5\ days in front-end tooling to 69.6\ days in physical signoff. (b) Relative to front-end logic synthesis, defects escaping into hardware-software interfaces (8.5×) and physical static timing analysis (STA) signoff (11.5×) multiply triage penalties.](images/fig-lifecycle-defect-latency.png){#fig-lifecycle-defect-latency width="95%" fig-alt="Two-panel empirical plot of 4,564 closed silicon issues. Left panel shows defect resolution latency distributions by stage on a log scale, from 22.5 days for tooling to 69.6 days for signoff. Right panel shows a bar chart of resolution latency multipliers versus front-end synthesis, escalating from 1.0 times to 11.5 times at physical static timing analysis signoff."}

The step-by-step latency escalation across intermediate milestones illuminates the physical and cognitive causes of this bottleneck. In front-end build harnesses and logic synthesis, localized diagnostics isolate syntax errors, lint failures, and type mismatches in minutes. As candidates advance to functional verification and macro floorplanning, debugging demands multi-cycle waveform inspection and spatial congestion analysis, expanding triage times by 4.5× to 5.8×. The steepest penalty occurs at cross-abstraction boundaries. Resolving defects at the hardware-software toolchain interface requires co-debugging compiler passes against microarchitectural state (8.5× latency multiplier), while physical static timing signoff imposes an 11.5× multiplier. At timing signoff, diagnosing a setup violation requires extracting high-dimensional parasitic resistance-capacitance networks, evaluating multiple process-voltage-temperature corners, and untangling gate-level netlists far removed from high-level architectural intent.

This steep latency escalation explains why AI-native exploration cannot afford to blindly generate RTL and delegate verification to late-stage physical signoff tools. Detecting and resolving a constraint mismatch during Formulate or Explore preserves engineering bandwidth; allowing an unvetted candidate to escape into place-and-route or multi-corner timing closure stalls the entire design loop.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Isolate Failure Domains for Repair"}
**The principle:** Separate design activities so that a failed result can be traced to the assumptions, artifacts, or checks that need revision.

**The application:** Use the available diagnostics to choose what to revisit, preserving earlier work whose assumptions still hold. When the cause is uncertain or spans several activities, investigate it before choosing a repair.
:::

Each stage answers a question that the next activity depends on. The sequence provides an initial reading order; feedback can send work back to any earlier stage.

1. **Formulate.** What should the design achieve? State the question, baseline, constraints, permitted changes, and checks that will judge the result.
2. **Explore.** What alternatives are worth testing? Generate or select candidates, including different hardware and software organizations when the question permits them.
3. **Implement.** How can each candidate be tested? Develop the required models, RTL, and software, and run the tools needed to examine them.
4. **Evaluate.** What do the results establish? Check that the observations are valid for the intended comparison, then determine which requirements are satisfied or still unresolved.
5. **Interpret.** Why did the design behave this way? Test explanations for gains and failures, and use what is learned to guide further design work.
6. **Commit.** What should happen next? Review the study and decide whether to advance a candidate, reject it, revise the study, or stop.

The operational layers introduced in @sec-moonshot (Layer 1 point assistance, Layer 2 closed-loop optimization within a frozen container, and Layer 3 AI-native design systems) differ in how learned components coordinate this work. A Layer 1 assistant might draft RTL during Implement. A Layer 2 optimizer might tune pipeline depth and buffer partitions within fixed block interfaces. A Layer 3 system generates alternative microarchitectural organizations, lowers their hardware and software together, and uses physical signoff feedback to guide structural redesign. Prediction, generation, and optimization can contribute across the stages; they are methods used within the workflow, rather than additional stages.

Suppose one candidate Lighthouse design uses an NPU for part of its extended reality (XR) workload, one of the compute options left open in @sec-moonshot. The walkthrough focuses on its accumulator block, which combines partial products into matrix-multiplication results. It asks how to improve throughput within the block's allocated timing and power limits in a 3\ nm-class design flow. The candidates, timing failure, and diagnosis are constructed teaching examples. Following one block through the six stages makes their connections concrete (@fig-ontology-loop).

![**The six-stage design life cycle carries system intent to a reviewed decision.** Execution advances systematically through Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit. Targeted repair routes unexpected outcomes back to re-evaluate the responsible stage, such as reopening formulation when targets prove physically unattainable, without restarting valid intermediate progress.](images/fig-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="80%" fig-alt="Life-cycle diagram of six stages arranged in two rows, with arrows from Formulate through Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, to Commit. One return arrow leads from the decision back to formulation."}

One application of the life cycle to a bounded architecture question is a *scoped study*. The NPU block study is one such application; it does not settle every question about the processor that contains it. The sequence runs from initial formulation to reviewed commitment, but its essential property is the return path: when evaluation or interpretation uncovers a constraint violation, targeted feedback routes the failure directly to the responsible stage rather than restarting the entire pipeline. Within the study, a design loop occurs when an empirical result changes the candidate microarchitecture or the plan itself and triggers another action, as defined in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales. Merely completing a predetermined parameter sweep without adaptive feedback does not constitute a design loop.

Studies can also depend on one another across hierarchy levels. A subsystem study sets the NPU block's 3\ W power and timing envelopes, while the block study discovers whether those allocations can sustain a viable accumulator organization. If no legal candidate closes timing, that shortfall routes back to re-evaluate the subsystem contract. The walkthrough traces this block study through all six stages before examining how to coordinate multiple coupled studies.

### Stage 1: Formulating Core Architecture Questions

Formulation turns a product goal into a question that an architecture study can answer. For the NPU block, "improve throughput" becomes a comparison with the existing accumulator on a specified matrix-multiplication workload. The study asks whether a different organization can process more results per unit time while meeting the target clock period, the block's allocated power and area budgets, and its required numerical behavior. The power allocation must leave room for the rest of the Lighthouse subsystem within its 3\ W envelope. These requirements give later measurements a purpose.

The baseline must be understood well enough to make that comparison meaningful. If it models memory service as instantaneous, for example, an apparent accumulator bottleneck may disappear when realistic contention is included. Formulation therefore identifies the reference design, workload phases, tool assumptions, and checks needed to trust the comparison. It also distinguishes requirements inherited from the surrounding system from choices the study may reconsider.

For this example, permitted changes include the accumulator organization, pipeline structure, and supporting software schedule; the block's external interface and required behavior remain fixed. This leaves room to generate a different design without silently changing the problem. The plan also sets a run budget and stopping conditions, including when to request review because a required change falls outside the agreed scope. The result of formulation is a testable question and a plan for answering it. Exploration can now propose alternatives against that plan.

### Stage 2: Exploring Alternatives

With the question and permitted changes established, exploration develops alternatives worth implementing. Some may tune the existing accumulator by changing pipeline depth or buffer partitions. Others may change its organization. A centralized accumulator connected through a wide crossbar, for example, can be compared with distributed accumulator banks that combine partial results through local connections. A generated proposal for the latter must also describe the control and software scheduling needed to deliver the required results.

These alternatives trade more than throughput. Additional parallel paths may require more storage and routing, while banking may reduce some long connections but introduce conflicts or extra reduction steps. The point of exploration is to expose these tradeoffs and choose informative candidates, not to certify physical feasibility from a high-level description. A simulator that omits wire delay[^fn-wire-delay-c03] could favor a wider crossbar for reasons that disappear in physical implementation. Predictions from such a model can help screen candidates only within the properties it represents.

[^fn-wire-delay-c03]: **Interconnect wire delay**: In advanced nanoscale fabrication nodes, wire resistance and parasitic capacitance scale unfavorably compared to transistor gate delays. Long interconnect wires across wide crossbars require repeater buffers and multi-cycle traversal, causing architectural models that assume single-cycle communication to systematically overestimate centralized crossbar throughput.

Choosing how to explore depends on what limits the study. If we have only a few accumulator designs, implementing and comparing them directly may be affordable. A larger study might use prediction to screen candidates, optimization to allocate evaluations, or generation to propose additional organizations. Each method brings costs and assumptions of its own. The choice is whether it helps answer the architecture question within the available budget, a comparison developed in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization.

The exploration history records why each candidate was selected or set aside. A proposal that violates a fixed interface can be rejected early; one whose timing is uncertain may deserve implementation because it tests a useful design hypothesis. Changes already permitted by the plan can proceed within the study. A proposal that requires a different system interface or power allocation returns to Formulate for review of the scope. The selected alternatives then move to Implement, where their hardware and software descriptions become testable.

### Stage 3: Implementing Testable Representations

A candidate organization needs a testable implementation before its proposed benefits can be assessed. For the NPU, this may involve a transaction-level model (TLM) of data movement, synthesizable RTL for the accumulator and its control, and a compiled software schedule that exercises the design. A TLM represents transfers as transactions rather than individual signal transitions, allowing some implementation detail to be deferred. Implementation develops these candidate artifacts together against an independently specified, immutable verification oracle (such as formal property assertions or an untuned golden reference model) that the generator is prohibited from modifying, preventing circular verification escapes. A banked accumulator is not a complete candidate if its software still assumes the centralized organization's access pattern.

Automated research toolchains such as OpenROAD Flow Scripts demonstrate scriptable logic synthesis, placement, and routing on open nodes [@OpenROADDocs], but 3\ nm-class commercial realization requires proprietary foundry-qualified design rule decks and signoff engines whose licensing and wall-clock latency prohibit unconstrained interactive execution. An early behavioral model can test an algorithm or schedule, while a physical timing estimate needs the appropriate implementation and electrical models. Choosing which design relationships to preserve at each level is the representation problem developed in @sec-data-representations-world-models.

Implementation also determines which verification checks to run first. Verification costs scale sharply across abstraction levels, ranging from sub-second syntax linting and rapid functional simulation to multi-hour static timing analysis and physical place-and-route. Efficient design workflows therefore use tiered screening to reject flawed candidates early before committing expensive physical implementation cycles.

An early check saves later work only when it can detect a reason to reject or repair the candidate. Passing that check leaves properties outside its scope unresolved. A behavioral simulation, for example, cannot establish that an implementation will meet the foundry's physical design rules.[^fn-drc-c03] Screening determines which candidates receive further implementation effort; it does not replace the checks needed for the final comparison.

[^fn-drc-c03]: **Design rule check (DRC)**: A check of layout geometry against manufacturing rules (such as minimum wire widths and spacing) enforced by the semiconductor foundry to guarantee physical manufacturability and yield. Passing behavioral simulation does not establish compliance with these rules.

Implementation also checks that the tools examined the intended candidate. A syntactically valid configuration can select the wrong top-level module, hold an active-low reset asserted, or skip the target workload phase. A generated block may pass isolated tests yet violate an interconnect handshake, omit required power-domain isolation,[^fn-power-domain-isolation-c03] or depend on the wrong compiler target. The candidate, supporting software, interface checks, and tool inputs must therefore remain linked throughout execution.

[^fn-power-domain-isolation-c03]: **Power-domain isolation**: Specialized clamp circuits placed at boundaries between independent voltage or power domains on a system-on-chip (SoC). When a block is powered off to eliminate static leakage, isolation cells hold boundary signals at defined logic levels (0 or 1) to prevent floating inputs and destructive short-circuit crowbar currents in neighboring active blocks.

A failed run needs diagnosis before it can inform a design choice. A license timeout supplies no timing result. An out-of-memory failure may reflect resource allocation, a tool problem, or a candidate whose implementation is unusually demanding. Recording what ran and what failed preserves these distinctions. Keeping that information consistent across automated runs and retries motivates the tool interfaces and run management developed in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces. Evaluate then asks what the completed checks can establish about the design.

### Stage 4: Evaluating Candidates

Once implementation confirms what executed, evaluation checks whether the returned results answer the planned question. Clean execution alone does not establish measurement validity. A power report produced for the wrong workload phase, for example, cannot establish power for the phase being compared. The candidate and baseline must be assessed under comparable conditions, with their required behavior checked before a performance gain is accepted. Several tools may be needed because no single model observes every relevant property.

Suppose a candidate with a wider centralized crossbar compiles cleanly and a C++ performance model predicts higher accumulator throughput at the target clock frequency. In the same hypothetical example, static timing analysis (STA)[^fn-sta-c03] reports a 150\ ps setup timing violation on the accumulator paths, while power-integrity analysis reports voltage drop ($IR$-drop) near critical buffers.[^fn-ir-drop-c03] Evaluation records that timing fails the declared constraint. The throughput prediction assumes a frequency that this implementation has not shown it can sustain, so the candidate cannot yet be accepted as an improvement.

[^fn-sta-c03]: **Static timing analysis (STA)**: An exhaustive verification method that calculates signal propagation delays across all circuit paths against clock constraints without dynamic simulation vectors. A setup timing violation indicates negative slack, meaning data arrives too late relative to the clock edge and the circuit cannot reliably operate at the target clock frequency.

[^fn-ir-drop-c03]: **IR drop**: A voltage decrease caused by current flowing through resistance in the power-distribution network. Reduced supply voltage can slow switching and contribute to timing violations.

Each requirement receives its own outcome: passed, failed, or unresolved. A passing functional check does not cancel the timing failure, and a missing power estimate remains unknown. The voltage-drop observation may help explain the failure, but it does not establish its cause. That is the question for Interpret.

### Stage 5: Interpreting Empirical Results

Evaluation establishes which requirements hold under the tested conditions. Both gains and failures still need interpretation, because the same measured change can arise from different mechanisms. Stage 5 asks which explanation the evidence supports and what observation would distinguish the remaining possibilities.

For the NPU, the architect must distinguish a long crossbar path from inadequate power delivery, sub-optimal cell sizing, or an incorrectly configured analysis. In standard physical design, a 150\ ps timing deficit is first triaged through local physical transformations: gate sizing, swapping to lower-threshold-voltage ($V_t$) cells, buffer insertion, or useful clock skew tuning. In leading-edge FinFET and nanosheet nodes (such as 3\ nm), however, aggressive $V_t$ swapping incurs steep exponential subthreshold leakage penalties ($I_{\text{sub}} \propto e^{-qV_t / kT}$) that quickly consume the tight 3\ W thermal envelope. If these physical optimizations fail to recover timing margin without violating leakage limits, the next level of repair evaluates microarchitectural retiming, such as inserting a pipeline register stage. Only when the timing wall reflects a fundamental physical floorplanning bottleneck, such as high interconnect resistance-capacitance (RC) delay across an overly centralized crossbar, does the evidence justify structural redesign.

An automated system assists by extracting critical timing paths, comparing cell-delay versus net-delay ratios, and proposing explanatory hypotheses.[^fn-credit-assignment-c03] Testing a shorter interconnect path or localized retiming under identical analysis settings helps isolate the contribution of wire delay. To prevent unbounded recursive simulation during automated root-cause analysis, counterfactual exploration must be bounded by a partitioned diagnostic compute sub-budget. Any accompanying changes in buffering, placement, or capacitive load must also be examined before attributing the improvement to one cause. Such a test requires another Implement execution and Evaluate comparison before Interpret can use the result.

If the evidence points to long shared global interconnect as the insurmountable limiting factor, exploration can revisit the distributed-bank alternative. The next iteration would develop its local reduction paths, control, and software schedule, then check timing, power, and numerical behavior again. Interpretation thus helps generate the next design. Deciding which observations justify that redesign, and which explanations still need testing, connects this stage to the verification and feedback methods developed in @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

[^fn-credit-assignment-c03]: **The architectural credit assignment problem**: In multi-stage closed-loop design, attributing a downstream physical failure (such as negative slack, routing congestion, or localized $IR$-drop) to an upstream design decision is a classic credit assignment challenge. A timing violation could originate from an over-aggressive clock constraint in Formulate, a poor microarchitectural topology in Explore, awkward coding style in Implement, or suboptimal seed initialization in physical synthesis. Resolving credit assignment requires automated sensitivity analysis and controlled counterfactual trials to isolate root causes before triggering expensive structural redesigns.

Automating this diagnosis remains a capability to demonstrate within the study's scope. A plausible generated explanation is a hypothesis until observations can distinguish it from alternatives. When they cannot, the study retains the competing explanations and either requests further investigation or stops for review. A useful outcome may be a supported design recommendation, but it may also be a clearer account of what remains unknown.

### Stage 6: Reviewing Evidence and Committing Decisions

Commit brings the study to a reviewed decision. The decision may be to advance a candidate, reject it, revise the question, or stop with unresolved issues. Here, "commit" means deciding what the completed work justifies doing next. The consequence depends on the study: advancing an NPU block to integration is different from approving a design for fabrication.

If a revised NPU block satisfies the declared checks, the responsible architect reviews whether it improves on the baseline and what remains to be checked in the larger system. A recommendation includes the tested design and software revisions, the comparison conditions, the explanation for the improvement, and remaining limitations. Passing this block study does not by itself authorize mask freeze.[^fn-mask-freeze-c03] If timing still fails, the architect can choose further work or close the study without selecting a candidate.

[^fn-mask-freeze-c03]: **Mask freeze**: The final signoff milestone (often termed tapeout) where physical layout geometries are locked and released to manufacture optical lithography reticles (photomasks). In advanced process nodes, a complete mask set costs tens of millions of dollars; unlike software patches, post-mask freeze silicon defects require an expensive and time-consuming physical respin.

Routine iterations can proceed automatically within the scope and budget established during Formulate. Review is needed when the planned decision is reached, the scope must change, or the stopping conditions call for it. This allows useful automation without treating each tool invocation as a separate approval event. Exhausting the run budget ends the permitted work; it does not establish that no feasible design exists.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="From the NPU block to the Lighthouse subsystem"}
**Context.** The accumulator study examines one block in a candidate Lighthouse design. Its results must eventually be evaluated in the XR workload that motivated the design.

**Application.** Faster accumulation may shorten a workload stage, but additional transfers or memory contention may erase that gain. The integrated comparison must check workload deadlines, the matching software schedule, and power across the subsystem, including memory and leakage.

**Outcome.** A successful block study could justify evaluating the revised NPU in the surrounding system. Whether that Lighthouse candidate meets its 3\ W target and real-time requirements remains a question for the subsystem study.
:::

::: {.callout-design-principle title="The Admission Test of an AI-Native System: The Honest Stop"}
**The principle:** A valid architectural outcome includes rejecting every candidate, retaining the baseline reference, or halting exploration before tool dispatch when available tools cannot observe target physical reality.

**The application:** In advanced commercial process nodes such as TSMC N3E, empirical academic tools like CACTI have zero physical validity for FinFET and nanosheet push-rule bitcells, multi-threshold leakage distributions, or write-assist circuits. When evaluation prerequisites or calibrated tool collateral are missing, an AI-native system must halt before dispatch rather than generating uncalibrated, fictional returns. Halting before dispatch preserves engineering integrity; manufacturing speculative numbers to satisfy an optimization loop is an architectural failure mode.
:::

The six stages can now serve as a reference for planning a study. Their inputs, outputs, and reasons to revisit earlier work differ, even when one person or tool performs several activities (@tbl-stage-seams).

| **Stage** | **Starts from** | **Produces** | **Reason to revisit** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Formulate** | Product goals and system requirements. | A question, baseline, scope, checks, and stopping conditions. | Evidence calls the target, assumptions, or permitted changes into question. |
| **Explore** | The plan and what earlier candidates taught. | Candidate organizations or configurations, with reasons for testing them. | A candidate fails, or a result suggests a better alternative. |
| **Implement** | A candidate and the checks it needs. | Testable hardware and software, tool inputs, and execution results. | Artifacts need revision, or the intended checks did not run. |
| **Evaluate** | Execution results and the planned comparison. | Valid comparisons and passed, failed, or unresolved checks. | Conditions are mismatched or observations are insufficient. |
| **Interpret** | Checked results and possible explanations. | Supported explanations, remaining hypotheses, and proposed investigations. | Causes remain uncertain or another result contradicts the explanation. |
| **Commit** | The plan, comparisons, explanations, and limitations. | A reviewed decision to advance, reject, revise, or stop. | Missing evidence or a changed requirement reopens the decision. |
: **Each stage contributes something different to a design decision.** The reference distinguishes what an activity needs, what it contributes, and why it may be revisited. A single failure can require work in several stages. {#tbl-stage-seams tbl-colwidths="[15,25,30,30]"}

Evaluate needs both the results from Implement and the criteria declared in Formulate; Commit needs the accumulated work, not only the last interpretation. Repair can also cross several boundaries. A timing violation may send a candidate back to Explore, while evidence that the target itself is infeasible may send the question back to Formulate. Preserving these connections lets another architect follow what happened and why.

## Design-Loop Cards and Documentation {#sec-design-loop-card}

Reviewing the NPU study requires more than its best timing report. Another architect needs to know which candidate produced it, which workload and constraints were used, why that candidate was selected, and what earlier failures taught the team. Much of this information may already exist in repositories, experiment logs, and verification reports. The documentation task is to connect it to the question and the resulting decision.

The book calls this connected account a *study record*. It includes the plan, candidate revisions, comparisons, explanations, failed or unfinished work, and the decision or stopping reason. An *execution record* supplies the details of a particular attempt: its inputs, tool environment, outputs, and status. The distinction matters in the NPU example. One execution record may show a timing violation; the study record explains how that observation led to another accumulator design. A retry retains the failed attempt and identifies what changed, rather than overwriting its directory and losing the reason for the new run.

Logs should retain the inputs and settings that affect a run, including random seeds when applicable, library versions, and diagnostic output. A shared scratch directory is insufficient if later attempts overwrite the information needed to explain an earlier result.

> **Design-loop card.** A concise, structured index that binds a scoped study's baseline, candidate space, execution budget, verification criteria, and reviewer identity before tool dispatch, while linking mutable execution records back to immutable intent [@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards; @GebruEtAl2021Datasheets]. It borrows the idea of contextual documentation from Model Cards and Datasheets for Datasets, linking existing engineering records without introducing an invasive project-wide documentation system.

Keeping the study question between the product goal and individual tool runs helps a reviewer trace how a local result bears on a larger architectural commitment (@fig-structured-layer-above-rtl). This three-tier hierarchy organizes information dependencies rather than imposing a rigid software framework.

![**Scoped studies connect system goals to implementation results.** An explicit intermediate layer positions the architecture question, constraints, and linked artifacts between high-level system intent and low-level execution tools (simulators, compilers, and electronic design automation (EDA) engines). This structured binding preserves provenance from raw tool returns to reviewed architectural commitments.](images/fig-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="72%" fig-alt="Diagram in which system intent and human judgment appear above a scoped architecture study, which links its question and artifacts to results from implementation tools below. Feedback connects the study to further design work and review."}

A raw cycle count, for example, is meaningless without its driving workload trace and simulator configuration. Similarly, a physical timing estimate requires the applicable process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners,[^fn-pvt-c03] calibrated library models, and explicit timing constraints specified in Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) files.[^fn-sdc-c03] In the scoped study layer, linked artifacts collect these tool returns into a common path, evaluating them against the under-review claim. If returned evidence reveals an unrecoverable timing violation, the dashed feedback path routes the shortfall directly back to revise the claim or study parameters before committing downstream resources. Retaining these bidirectional bindings allows a reviewer to distinguish a simulated cycle improvement from a design that satisfies physical DRC and STA signoff, while making immediately visible which downstream comparisons must rerun when an upstream assumption shifts.

[^fn-pvt-c03]: **Process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners**: Combinations of device-model and operating assumptions used to check a design under different conditions. The limiting combination can differ across timing and power checks.

[^fn-sdc-c03]: **Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC)**: A format for specifying clocks, input and output delays, timing exceptions, and related constraints used by synthesis and timing-analysis tools.

Within the same Lighthouse design, a separate study could compare 2, 3, and 4\ MiB Level-2 (L2) cache capacities while holding the other architecture choices fixed. The question is whether fewer capacity misses reduce frame-time tail latency on the selected XRBench workload while meeting power, area, and access-time constraints. Power estimates must include leakage within the subsystem's 3\ W envelope. This memory comparison complements the accumulator study; each examines a different part of the system.

The cache example begins with an explicit plan before any simulation launches. The study names the baseline, candidates, physical checks, and intended commitment criteria. Direct enumeration is sufficient to compare the three capacities; this limited study does not require a learned method or demonstrate AI-native redesign by itself. It illustrates the structured documentation that also governs more complex generated alternatives.

A cycle-level simulator would estimate frame times, while a static random-access memory (SRAM) model[^fn-sram-model-c03] would estimate the arrays' area, power, and access time. Checking the subsystem envelope also requires the other components' power contributions. Each tool therefore supplies part of the comparison, and the card links those parts to the same candidate and workload.

[^fn-sram-model-c03]: **SRAM memory models**: Dense multi-megabyte cache arrays use custom analog-digital bitcells and sense amplifiers that cannot be efficiently synthesized from standard logic gates. Architectural exploration relies on analytical tools (such as CACTI) or foundry memory compilers to evaluate area, access latency, dynamic read and write energy, and static leakage for specific banking configurations.

Capturing the study plan in a structured, machine-readable design-loop card ensures that automated optimization loops and human reviewers share explicit assumptions before tool dispatch (@fig-filled-design-loop-card). The card binds the baseline, candidate space, execution budget, and evaluation criteria into a versioned contract, ensuring that empty result fields remain unpopulated until executed checks return verified telemetry.

![**A study card separates planned work from results and decisions.** Structured schema for the prospective Lighthouse Level-2 (L2) cache comparison. The four-execution budget and verification checks bind upfront intent before dispatch, while evidence fields and commitment decisions remain open until empirical telemetry returns.](images/fig-filled-design-loop-card){#fig-filled-design-loop-card width="75%" fig-alt="Illustration of a study card for a prospective XR cache study. A hypothesis precedes entries for the baseline, candidates, checks, execution budget, evidence needed, and responsible reviewer. No completed result is reported."}

The four-execution budget allocates one trial for each capacity candidate (2, 3, and 4\ MiB) with room for exactly one rerun. This hard budget ceiling reflects physical computing realities: running cycle-accurate simulations and detailed SRAM array modeling across extended workloads is computationally expensive. If an execution aborts due to tool timeouts, or if measured 99th-percentile tail latency cannot resolve statistical variance within the four allocated runs, the card enforces the Honest Stop: the outcome stays strictly unresolved rather than manufacturing speculative conclusions. Although the accumulator and cache studies address the same prospective subsystem, their modular cards keep their failure domains separate. Adopting an altered NPU accumulator changes interconnect traffic and thermal dissipation, requiring the architect to revisit the cache card with updated background power assumptions.


The accumulator and cache studies also show why these technical choices must be made together. A representation that permits only buffer-capacity changes cannot express a distributed accumulator organization, even if a generator proposes one. A more flexible representation would still need a tool path that can test the generated design and observations that can guide its revision.

The following chapters develop these connections. @sec-data-representations-world-models examines what design and workload information methods need to use; @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization asks which methods can help answer a particular architecture question at acceptable cost. Reliable execution of the chosen checks is developed in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, and the interpretation and use of their results in @sec-feedback-verification-trust. These ingredients serve several stages rather than matching the stages one for one, providing the foundation for cross-stack loop composition (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack) and hands-on laboratory execution.

## Open Questions

The six stages provide a way to organize a study, but they do not establish how much separation is useful or how work should be revisited as results arrive. The accumulator and cache studies expose these choices both within a study and between related block and subsystem studies.

- **How much separation between activities helps the complete study?** Distinct stages can make assumptions and unfinished work visible, but enforcing a separate handoff for every activity may add waiting, translation, and duplicated checks. A small block study and a coordinated hardware–software redesign may need different arrangements. The useful test is whether an arrangement improves the time and effort needed to reach a sound decision, including the cost of coordination. The six-stage framework helps describe what is being compared; it does not predetermine the best implementation.

- **How should a workflow choose which work to revisit after a failed result?** The NPU timing violation could call for revised physical implementation, a different accumulator organization, or correction of the analysis constraints. The stage descriptions distinguish these activities, but the diagnostic may not establish which action will be useful. Revisiting too little can preserve a mistaken assumption, while restarting the whole study can discard valid work. How can an automated workflow choose a productive next step within its budget while recognizing when interacting causes require coordinated changes or human investigation?

- **When should results reopen the original question?** Repeated timing failures do not prove that the NPU target is infeasible. They may justify another organization, a different experiment, or review of the target itself. An analytical bound can sometimes rule out a target under stated assumptions without testing every candidate. A study may also discover that its objective poorly represents the product goal, even when individual candidates pass. What evidence should trigger reconsideration of Formulate, and how can the workflow distinguish a justified revision from relaxing the requirements merely to obtain a passing result?

- **When should related block studies be reconsidered together?** The accumulator and cache comparisons begin as separate studies, yet changing either design can alter the conditions under which the other was evaluated. A faster accumulator may alter memory traffic, while a cache choice may change the power available to compute. Repeating affected checks can reveal a conflict without establishing whether to revise one block, reallocate power within the subsystem, or reconsider the organization as a whole. How should the workflow decide when separate studies remain useful and when the architecture question needs joint reconsideration?

## Summary

The life cycle connects an architecture question to candidate generation, implementation, comparison, interpretation, and a reviewed decision. In the NPU example, a promising throughput prediction led to physical checks, a timing failure, and investigation of another accumulator organization. Progress came from connecting what each activity learned to what the next one needed. The sequence can repeat, overlap, or return to the original question as the study develops.

This organization gives the rest of the book a common framework while leaving its practical implementation open. A small cache comparison may use direct enumeration; a broader AI-native study may generate and develop different hardware–software organizations. Both need meaningful comparisons and an account of what the results justify. The amount of automation can change without removing those engineering needs.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Begin with a testable question.** The baseline, requirements, permitted changes, and stopping conditions make later comparisons meaningful while leaving room for alternative organizations.
- **Connect generation to implementation.** A proposed organization needs a representation that can express it, along with matching hardware, software, and checks before its benefits can be assessed.
- **Separate evaluation from interpretation.** Establish what passed, failed, or remains unknown, then investigate why and use the findings to guide another design.
- **Revisit the work affected by a result.** Preserve earlier results whose assumptions still hold, and investigate coupled causes before selecting a repair.
- **Keep the decision proportional to the evidence.** Retain the conditions, attempts, and limitations needed for review. Advancing, rejecting, revising, and stopping unresolved are all possible outcomes; budget exhaustion does not prove infeasibility.
:::

To generate and compare the accumulator alternatives, a method needs descriptions that expose their different organizations while retaining the workload and constraints. @sec-data-representations-world-models examines how to represent that information, beginning with the architectural data from which those descriptions are built.
